before: out T means a generic producer may expose T in output positions without accepting it as an ordinary input. This permits a Source<String> to be used as Source<Any>. in T supports the complementary consumer direction; variance does not mean deep immutability.

MutableList<out Number> is a use-site projection: it accepts a mutable list whose actual element type is some subtype of Number. Reading as Number is safe, but adding an arbitrary Number is not: the original list might allow only Int. The underlying list may still be mutated through another valid reference.

Complete local Kotlin/JVM example; the app itself does not execute it:
```kotlin
class Source<out T>(val value: T)
fun first(values: MutableList<out Number>): Number = values[0]
fun main() {
    val source: Source<Any> = Source("ok")
    val numbers = mutableListOf(3, 5)
    println(source.value)
    println(first(numbers))
}
```

Expected output or behavior: ok

after: Variance describes when one generic type can stand in for another. A class declared with `out T` gives out T values without accepting them as ordinary inputs. A source of Strings can therefore be read as a source of Any values.

The type `MutableList<out Number>` gives a restricted view, called a projection. It may refer to a list of Ints or another Number subtype. You can read an item as Number, but cannot add an arbitrary Number because the list's exact item type is hidden.

Follow the example one line at a time.
```kotlin
class Source<out T>(val value: T)
fun first(values: MutableList<out Number>): Number = values[0]
fun main() {
    val source: Source<Any> = Source("ok")
    val numbers = mutableListOf(3, 5)
    println(source.value)
    println(first(numbers))
}
```
The screen shows `ok`, then `3`. Reading the first number is safe: an Int is a Number. Adding a Double through this view would not be safe for the original Int list.
The word `in` supports the other direction: accepting values as inputs. These type rules control access, not whether an object can ever change. Another valid reference may still change the same list.

before.question: If first tries values.add(2.5) before returning values[0], what happens?
choices: Compilation rejects adding through the projected list.
It adds a Double to every Int list safely.
It changes Source to an input-only type.
before.explanation: The projection hides the exact allowed subtype; a Double might violate the original Int list’s element contract.

after.question: Inside first, try `values.add(2.5)` before reading the first item. What happens?
choices: Compilation fails because this view cannot add that value.
It safely adds a Double to any Int list.
It makes Source accept inputs only.
after.explanation: The actual list may accept only Int values. The out view hides that exact type, so adding a Double is rejected.
